title: Great Leaders Know When to Follow
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that a critical, underappreciated leadership move is deliberately stepping back to serve as a team member rather than the leader on a given initiative. It distinguishes this from simply deferring to expertise, describing instead a leader who appoints someone else to lead a temporary team and genuinely follows their direction. The piece frames this willingness to give up control as a powerful signal of humility and self-awareness that strengthens trust and models the behavior leaders hope to see from everyone else on the team.
points: Knowing when to follow rather than lead is a critical, underappreciated leadership skill.
This goes beyond deferring to expertise — it means genuinely appointing someone else as leader and becoming a team member.
The humility this requires strengthens trust and elevates a leader's credibility with the team.
No leader possesses the deepest expertise on every issue, making occasional followership a practical necessity.
Leaders who follow well model the behavior they hope to see from everyone else on the team.
quotes: A critically important moment in any team occurs when a leader is wise enough to know that they need to follow instead of lead on an issue or initiative.
The humility, confidence, and self-awareness that becoming a follower projects serve to elevate the leader’s credibility and create a trusted bond with the team.
No leader possesses the deepest knowledge, skill, and expertise about all issues and topics.
Leaders who believe a lack of authority prevents them from being effective need to rethink their understanding of leadership.
Followers will always be more important to leaders than leaders are to followers.
